Field studies of Yuma myotis (Myotis yumanensis) have begun to clarify the species' fundamental metabolic requirements under controlled laboratory conditions. Respirometry trials conducted on post-absorptive individuals at rest revealed that basal oxygen consumption reaches approximately 13.50 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = approximately 13.50 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at a body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This metabolic rate is comparable to values reported for other small-bodied vespertilionid bats, reflecting the considerable energetic demands of maintaining endothermy at such a diminutive size. The standardized measurement conditions, involving a thermoneutral zone assessment, ensure that the recorded oxygen consumption represents true basal metabolism rather than activity-related costs. Understanding this baseline energetic requirement is critical for modeling the daily energy budgets of free-ranging individuals, particularly given the species' reliance on insect prey that fluctuates seasonally in abundance.

Reproductive output in Myotis yumanensis is constrained by an annual cycle typical of temperate-zone vespertilionids, with females producing a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and that litter being born just once each year [F_R_i = litter being born just once each year]. This modest annual fecundity, measured under the thermal conditions of a 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C] roosting environment, represents a life-history strategy in which parental investment is concentrated into a single, relatively well-developed offspring per breeding season. The reliance on only one reproductive event per annum is characteristic of many insectivorous bats that face pronounced seasonal constraints on prey availability and must balance the energetic costs of lactation against the necessity of accumulating fat reserves for winter hibernation. This low reproductive rate places Yuma myotis among the slower-reproducing small mammals, a demographic trait that renders local populations particularly vulnerable to disturbances that elevate adult mortality rates.

Neonatal development begins with parturition, at which point the altricial pup weighs a mere 0.79 grams [Wwb = 0.79 grams], a remarkably light birth mass indicative of the species' extreme precocial-in-altricial continuum where newborns are tiny but capable of clinging to the mother. This wet weight at birth represents only a small fraction of the ultimate adult body mass that females will eventually attain. Over the course of postnatal growth, female Yuma myotis reach a maximum adult body mass of 6.75 grams [Wwi = 6.75 grams], a value that aligns with the typical 5 to 7 gram range reported in reference works and represents the asymptotic size achieved once skeletal and muscular development are complete. The dramatic increase from neonatal to adult mass underscores the intensity of the suckling period and the subsequent juvenile foraging phase, during which pups must more than octuple their birth weight while relying entirely on maternal milk and later on progressively independent insect hunting.

The gestation period for Myotis yumanensis has been documented under stable thermal conditions in captive maternity colonies, where pregnant females maintained at 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C] carry their developing offspring for a mean duration of 54 days [tg = 54 days]. This length of pregnancy is typical for a bat of this body size, balancing the need for thorough organogenesis with the seasonal imperative to time parturition with peak insect availability in late spring. Delays or accelerations in gestation may occur if females enter torpor during cold spells, but under the consistent warm temperatures provided in captivity, the 54-day interval serves as a reliable benchmark for the species' reproductive schedule. Following birth, the neonatal pup remains entirely dependent on its mother's milk for nourishment during an initial period of rapid growth, with complete nutritional independence occurring relatively early in the developmental timeline.

The transition to full nutritional independence, or weaning, occurs at 35 days after birth [tx = 35 days after birth] under the same 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C] thermal regime that characterizes active roosting conditions. At this stage, the now volant juvenile begins capturing its own insect prey, though it may continue to receive supplemental milk from the mother for some additional days. Sexual maturation proceeds more gradually: females attain puberty at 365 days after birth [tp = 365 days after birth], meaning that first ovulation typically occurs in the spring following their birth year, at approximately one year of age at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. Consequently, the maximum lifespan in the wild has been estimated at 14 years [am = 14 years] for individuals capable of surviving the cumulative risks of predation, food shortages, and hibernation, a longevity that underscores the slow-paced, high-survivorship life history that compensates for the species' exceptionally low annual reproductive output at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C].
